assessment.nobel_worthiness: The magic-wavelength optical lattice clock combines an original idea (Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation of many atoms at once) with a decisive leap in precision, now at the 1e-18 level. It opens fundamental tests (constancy of constants, relativistic redshift over millimetres) and is a clear instance of deep atomic-physics understanding translating into new measurement capability.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated it first; Jun Ye's group brought the strontium clock to record accuracy and coherence and developed the many-body (spin-exchange) understanding. Both contributions are decisive and the two-person configuration looks fair. Others (e.g. Lemonde, Hollberg, Hall's frequency-comb work already recognised in 2005) are not in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories worldwide run lattice clocks, comparisons agree, and the redefinition of the second is being prepared around such clocks. Recognition would be timely, with the field well confirmed.
uncertainties: Whether the committee regards this as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes on frequency combs and ion control.
Relative weight of Katori's original proposal versus Ye's later precision milestones; I rely on memory for the detailed chronology.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms turns the wave nature of massive particles into a precision sensor for gravity, rotation and the fine-structure constant. It is conceptually simple, original and pedagogically powerful, and it probes the quantum-classical boundary directly while giving measurable results.
assessment.attribution: Bordé introduced the atom-interferometer theory and the Ramsey-Bordé scheme, Pritchard pioneered atom optics and first interferometers with atoms and molecules, and Kasevich (with Chu) demonstrated light-pulse gravimeters and gyroscopes. The three-person set is plausible, though Steven Chu and others (Mlynek, Keith, Ketterle's related work) are credited elsewhere or absent from this list, so the allocation is not fully clean.
assessment.maturity: Atom gravimeters and gradiometers are commercial and used in geodesy, and measurements of G and alpha have been reproduced by several groups. The technique is mature; the large-scale tests (equivalence principle, gravitational waves) are still ongoing.
uncertainties: Overlap with Chu's 1997 laser-cooling recognition and with the 2001 condensate prize may make the committee reluctant.
Priority among early demonstrations (Pritchard, Mlynek, Kasevich-Chu, Bordé) is contested; I am recalling this from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposals showed how cold trapped ions and neutral atoms could implement quantum gates and analogue simulation of many-body Hamiltonians. This theory shaped an entire experimental field in atomic physics and quantum information, with lasting influence and high originality.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the two evident theorists with joint, decisive proposals (1995 ion-trap gate; 1998 Bose-Hubbard in lattices with Jaksch et al.). The two-person credit is clean, as they are single-handedly associated with the key ideas. Jaksch, Briegel and others share part of the lattice work, which is not credited here.
assessment.maturity: The ion-trap gate has been realised and scaled in several laboratories, and optical-lattice quantum simulators have become a standard platform. Experimental confirmation is extensive, though the large-scale usefulness of quantum simulation is still developing.
uncertainties: Prizes in 2012 (Wineland, Haroche) and 2022 already covered nearby territory, so novelty relative to those awards may be questioned.
The compound nature (ion-trap computing versus lattice simulation) might call for separate recognition of experimentalists such as Blatt and Bloch.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry's geometric phase reveal that potentials and global phase structure have physical consequences even where fields vanish. This is a genuinely new understanding of quantum mechanics that now underlies Berry curvature, topological matter, adiabatic pumping and molecular conical intersections, and is exactly the kind of foundational insight I value.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959; Bohm deceased) are the originators of the effect, and Berry (1984) generalised it to adiabatic phases; Aharonov and Anandan later extended it. Using Aharonov and Berry is defensible but leaves Bohm, Pancharatnam, Anandan and Simon, so the credit is partial and could be seen as unfair.
assessment.maturity: Tonomura's electron-holography experiments, Berry-phase measurements in many systems and countless applications confirm the physics beyond doubt. If anything the recognition is late, and the surviving laureate candidates are elderly.
uncertainties: A two-person prize cannot reflect Bohm's role, and the Nobel statutes exclude posthumous awards.
Whether the committee sees this as a discovery or invention in the statutory sense, since it is largely a theoretical concept with later experimental confirmation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Prediction and observation of the quantum spin Hall state introduced a new classification of electronic matter based on topology, with protected edge channels. It is original, clear and has changed how a large part of condensed matter physics is organised, though I defer to colleagues who work in that area.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele provided the theoretical identification (Z2 invariant) and Molenkamp's group the first experimental demonstration in HgTe quantum wells after the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction. Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore and Balents are not in this credit, so allocation is contested, and the 2016 prize also touched on topological phases.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in multiple materials and by several groups, with a large follow-up literature; recognition is not premature. The distance from the 2016 topological-phase prize might need justification.
uncertainties: Open priority question around the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the 3D topological insulator discoveries.
I am outside my field here and weigh condensed-matter priority disputes with less confidence.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bringing visible mechanical objects with billions of atoms into the quantum ground state and entangling or squeezing them speaks directly to where the quantum world ends and the everyday world begins. The experiments are clean and fundamental and combine cavity and circuit techniques.
assessment.attribution: Cleland and colleagues achieved the first mechanical ground-state cooling and quantum control in the circuit regime, Teufel the sideband ground-state cooling and strong coupling in microwave optomechanics, and Aspelmeyer the cavity optomechanics programme and entanglement of massive oscillators. Others (Painter, Kippenberg, Regal, Lehnert, O'Connell) made comparable contributions, so a cut at three is somewhat arbitrary.
assessment.maturity: Many groups reproduce ground-state cooling, squeezing and entanglement, and applications to sensing and gravitational-wave detection exist. It is plausible but still a bit young as a recognised discovery, and the 2025 prize on macroscopic tunnelling in circuits touches the same theme.
uncertainties: Difficult attribution among several leaders; the three listed names might not be the decisive ones.
Proximity to the 2025 prize may lower urgency.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed states beat the standard quantum limit in interferometers and demonstrate how quantum noise can be engineered. Caves' 1981 analysis and the later experiments show quantum optics making a real difference in precision measurement, now in the LIGO detectors.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the key theory, Kimble's group made early squeezed-light experiments and cavity-QED work, and Schnabel led the implementation in gravitational-wave detectors such as GEO600. Slusher and colleagues' first squeezing observation and Walls, Yuen and others are not credited, so the set is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Squeezing is now routine in LIGO, Virgo and GEO, which is strong independent confirmation. Because the gravitational-wave detection already received recognition in 2017, the committee might think the connection supports it, though attribution complexity remains.
uncertainties: Whether the decisive credit sits with Caves, Slusher, Kimble or the detector-implementation teams.
The key early experimental attribution is from memory and may be imprecise.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 and entanglement-based key distribution turned quantum measurement and non-locality into a protocol for secure communication. The ideas are original and clear and connect to the Bell-test physics already recognised in 2022, although the work is more an information-theoretic invention than a new physical phenomenon.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard authored BB84, and Ekert authored the entanglement-based E91 protocol, so a three-person prize is natural. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea and the experimental realisation by others are not credited, leaving some unresolved fairness issues.
assessment.maturity: Quantum key distribution has been demonstrated over fibre and satellite links by multiple groups and is partly commercial, although practical security loopholes remain active. The theory has been stable for decades, so the timing is not premature.
uncertainties: Questionable fit to a physics Nobel prize as the contribution is conceptual and partly computer science.
Duplicate-like entry B014 includes the same names with a teleportation emphasis; I have not used it so as to avoid double counting.
